old.name: George Ryan
old.description:
George Ryan was an IWW member. George Ryan received a five-year prison sentence, which he served in San Quentin from November 1921 to January 1926. 107 R. J. Sanchez served a prison sentence in San Quentin, where he contracted tuberculosis. He was released in June 1924 on the condition that he would be deported.

George W. Ryan, of Leesburg, Virginia, was a Leesburg citizen held as a hostage for civilians captured by Mosby. He was held as a civilian political prisoner at Fort Delaware during the U.S. Civil War, detained without trial under the wartime suspension of habeas corpus, and is named among the fellow prisoners in the Rev. Isaac W. K. Handy's 1863–1864 prison diary, 'United States Bonds; or, Duress by Federal Authority.'

The June 1925 labor-press political-prisoner birthday notice lists him at San Quentin under prisoner number 35567, with a June 25 birthday (no birth year is given).

updates.description: George Ryan was a member of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) imprisoned at San Quentin, California. He received a five-year sentence under California criminal-syndicalism law and was confined from November 1921 to January 1926. Contemporary labor newspapers identify him as San Quentin prisoner 35567. A June 1925 political-prisoner birthday notice gives June 25 as his birthday but does not establish a birth year.
updates.body: Sources: Stephen M. Kohn, American Political Prisoners (1994), p. 166; The New Leader, July 18, 1925; and contemporary San Quentin prisoner rosters. The former Civil War material concerns a different person, George W. Ryan of Leesburg, Virginia.

new.name: George W. Ryan
new.description: George W. Ryan was a civilian from Leesburg, Virginia, held at Fort Delaware during the American Civil War. In his diary entry for August 22, 1864, fellow prisoner Isaac W. K. Handy named Ryan among the Leesburg civilians held as hostages for civilians captured by Mosby. He was detained without a criminal trial.
new.body: Source: Isaac W. K. Handy, United States Bonds (1874), p. 517, August 22, 1864 diary entry. This is the Leesburg civilian, distinct from George Ryan, the IWW prisoner held at San Quentin in the 1920s.

iww_case.charges: Federal prosecution under the Espionage Act of 1917 and/or the Sedition Act of 1918.

iww_updates.charges: California Criminal Syndicalism Act prosecution associated with IWW activity.
iww_updates.sentence: Five years in state prison; confined at San Quentin from November 1921 to January 1926.

civil_case.charges: A Leesburg citizen held as a hostage.

unrelated_ryans.name: Jeremy J. Ryan
unrelated_ryans.description: On June 26, 2020 Jeremy J. Ryan, 31, of Madison, WI was charged with making terrorist threats and stalking (both felonies) plus other misdemeanors for allegedly threatening to release personal information about Dane County Sheriff Dave Mahoney and his family and calling on protestors to harass Mahoney's family home. Sentenced to 3 months in Wisconsin state prison.

unrelated_ryans.name: Jack Ryan
unrelated_ryans.description: Jack Ryan was a CIO organizer during the 1941 International Harvester strike in the Chicago area. When police raided the CIO strike headquarters without warrants, breaking down the door, Ryan was beaten and arrested with seventeen other strikers; the group was held incommunicado for two days before being booked on disorderly-conduct charges.

unrelated_ryans.name: Sheila P. Ryan
unrelated_ryans.description: Sheila P. Ryan joined the first recorded sit-in inside the White House on March 11, 1965, demanding federal protection for voting-rights marchers after Bloody Sunday in Selma. After refusing repeated orders to leave, the demonstrators were arrested at about 6 p.m. and convicted of unlawful entry; the D.C. Court of Appeals affirmed the convictions in 1966.
